fact: The Inca citadel sits at about 2,430 m on a ridge above the Urubamba River valley.
Africa's highest mountain, 5,895 m, rises alone from the plains near the Kenya-Tanzania border.
The city is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon.
The pyramid-shaped peak, 4,478 m high, stands on the border of Switzerland and Italy. It was first climbed in 1865.

q: Where is Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in the Alps?
fact: Mont Blanc rises about 4,806 m in the Alps between France and Italy. A road tunnel 11.6 km long runs right under it.
Its 307 m cliff is often called Europe's northern tip. In summer the sun does not set there for more than two months.

q: Where is the Strait of Gibraltar?
fact: Only about 14 km of water separate Europe from Africa here, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea.
The stone circle was built in stages between about 3000 and 1500 BC. Its big sarsen stones weigh about 25 tons on average.

q: Where is the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
fact: Work began in 1173, and the bell tower started to lean within a few years because the ground beneath it is soft.
The abbey stands on a tidal island. The tides in its bay are among the strongest in Europe, rising up to about 14 m.
Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman town in ash in AD 79. The ash preserved streets, houses, paintings and even loaves of bread.
Architect Antoni Gaudi worked on the city's Sagrada Familia basilica for over 40 years, until his death in 1926.
King Ludwig II of Bavaria began the fairy-tale castle in 1869. It inspired the Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland.
Geneva is home to the Red Cross, founded there in 1863, and to the main European offices of the United Nations.

q: Where is Rotterdam, Europe's largest seaport?
fact: Ships reach the port through the delta where the Rhine and the Maas flow into the North Sea.
This deep Scottish lake holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales put together.
About 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, most of them six-sided, formed here as lava cooled some 60 million years ago.

q: Where is Olympia, home of the ancient Olympic Games?
fact: The ancient Games were held here from 776 BC. The flame for every modern Olympics is still lit at Olympia.
This dormant volcano in the Caucasus rises to 5,642 m and is often counted as the highest mountain in Europe.
Peter the Great founded the city in 1703. It was Russia's capital for about 200 years.

q: Where is Geysir, the hot spring that gave all geysers their name?
fact: Geysir itself rarely erupts now, but its neighbor Strokkur shoots water about 20 m high every few minutes.

q: Where is Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe?
fact: A monument on the cliff quotes the poet Camoes: here 'the land ends and the sea begins'.

q: Where does the Danube River flow into the Black Sea?
fact: The Danube flows through or along 10 countries, more than any other river, and passes four capitals on the way.

q: Where is Rovaniemi, the 'hometown of Santa Claus'?
fact: The Arctic Circle runs just north of this town in Finnish Lapland. Visitors cross the line painted at Santa Claus Village.

q: Where is Salzburg, the city where Mozart was born?
fact: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born here in 1756. The film 'The Sound of Music' was also shot in and around the city.
This palace and fortress in Granada was built mainly in the 13th and 14th centuries by the Nasrid rulers of al-Andalus.

q: Where is Longyearbyen, on the Arctic islands of Svalbard?
fact: It is one of the world's northernmost towns. The Global Seed Vault, a backup store of the world's crop seeds, is dug into a mountain nearby.
Istanbul spans two continents: the Bosphorus strait splits the city between Europe and Asia.

q: Where is Cappadocia, the land of 'fairy chimneys'?
fact: Wind and rain carved the soft volcanic rock into tall cones. People dug homes and churches into them, and hot-air balloons now float above.
Japan's highest mountain, 3,776 m, is a volcano. It last erupted in 1707.
Kyoto was Japan's imperial capital for more than 1,000 years, from 794 until 1868, and has around 2,000 temples and shrines.
Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the white marble tomb in Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It took about 20 years.
India's financial center is also home to Bollywood, one of the busiest film industries in the world.
The world's highest mountain is 8,849 m tall, a height Nepal and China announced together in 2020. The border runs over its summit.

q: Where is K2, the second-highest mountain on Earth?
fact: K2 rises 8,611 m in the Karakoram range. It is considered much harder to climb than Everest.
Built in the early 12th century, it is the largest religious monument in the world - and it appears on Cambodia's flag.
Around 1,600 limestone islands and islets rise from the bay's green water. The name means 'where the dragon descends'.
The Nabataeans carved its temples and tombs straight into pink sandstone cliffs about 2,000 years ago.
Its shore, more than 400 m below sea level, is the lowest land on Earth. The water is so salty that people float without trying.
Dubai's Burj Khalifa, 828 m tall, has been the tallest building in the world since it opened in 2010.
Mecca is the holiest city of Islam. Millions of pilgrims travel there each year for the Hajj.
Thousands of life-size clay soldiers guard the tomb of China's first emperor. Farmers digging a well found them in 1974.
Shanghai has the busiest container port in the world, a title it has held every year since 2010.
Built on the island of Java in the 9th century, it is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, with 504 Buddha statues.

q: Where is the island of Bali?
fact: Most people on Bali are Hindu, unlike most of Indonesia, which has the world's largest Muslim population.
It is home to the Komodo dragon, the largest lizard in the world, which can grow to 3 m long.
More than 1,200 cone-shaped hills cover part of Bohol island. In the dry season their grass turns brown, like chocolate.
One of the great Silk Road cities, Samarkand is famous for the Registan, a square framed by three tiled madrasas.
In the 5th century, King Kashyapa built a palace on top of this rock, which rises about 180 m above the forest.
Darius the Great founded it around 518 BC as the ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire.
The world's first and largest spaceport. Yuri Gagarin, the first person in space, launched from here in 1961.

q: Where is the Tiger's Nest monastery?
fact: Paro Taktsang clings to a cliff about 900 m above the Paro valley. Legend says a guru flew there on the back of a tigress.
The deepest lake on Earth, about 1,640 m, holds roughly a fifth of all the fresh water in the world's lakes and rivers.

q: Where are the Pyramids of Giza?
fact: The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
In the 1960s the two temples of Ramesses II were cut into blocks and moved uphill, to save them from the rising Lake Nasser.
Opened in 1869, the canal links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea and spares ships the long trip around Africa.

q: Where is the Valley of the Kings?
fact: Pharaohs were buried in rock-cut tombs here. Tutankhamun's tomb, full of treasure, was found in 1922.

q: Where does the Nile River flow into the Mediterranean Sea?
fact: Before reaching the sea, the Nile fans out into a wide, fertile delta and splits into two main branches.
The Zambezi drops over a cliff 1.7 km wide on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border. Its local name means 'the smoke that thunders'.
Africa's largest lake is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. The Nile leaves the lake at Jinja, in Uganda.
Six hundred years ago it was a famous center of trade and learning, where scholars copied and wrote thousands of books by hand.

q: Where is the Great Mosque of Djenne?
fact: It is the largest mud-brick building in the world. Each year the whole town helps to cover its walls with fresh mud.
This stone city, built from the 11th to 15th centuries without mortar, gave its name to the modern country.

q: Where is the Cape of Good Hope?
fact: Despite its fame, it is not Africa's southern tip. That is Cape Agulhas, about 150 km to the east-southeast.

q: Where is Cape Agulhas, the southernmost point of Africa?
fact: By the official definition, the Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet here.
Gold was found here in 1886, and within a few years a mining camp grew into South Africa's largest city.
The 'Red City' is named for its walls of red earth. Storytellers, musicians and food stalls fill its main square every night.
The Okavango River never reaches the sea. It spreads into a huge green delta in the Kalahari, where most of its water evaporates.

q: Where is Sossusvlei, with its giant red dunes?
fact: Some dunes in this part of the Namib Desert are more than 300 m high, among the tallest on Earth.
One of the largest unbroken volcanic calderas in the world, about 19 km across. Lions, elephants and rhinos live on its floor.

q: Where is Lalibela, with its rock-cut churches?
fact: Eleven churches were carved down into the solid rock here in the 12th and 13th centuries. They are still used for worship.

q: Where is the Avenue of the Baobabs?
fact: A dirt road on Madagascar's west coast is lined with giant baobabs up to 30 m tall, some of them hundreds of years old.
Lagos is Nigeria's largest city. It was the capital until 1991, when the government moved to Abuja.

q: Where does the Congo River reach the Atlantic Ocean?
fact: The Congo is the deepest river in the world, more than 220 m in places, and carries more water than any river except the Amazon.
Each year, from about July to October, more than a million wildebeest arrive here from Tanzania's Serengeti.

q: Where is Dallol, in the Danakil Depression?
fact: Dallol lies below sea level and is one of the hottest places on Earth. Its acid hot springs are bright yellow, green and orange.
About 275 separate falls line nearly 3 km of the Iguazu River, on the border of Argentina and Brazil.
The Colorado River carved the canyon over millions of years. It is about 446 km long and up to 1.8 km deep.
Three falls sit on the Niagara River, between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, on the border of Canada and the United States.
Opened in 1914, the canal uses locks to lift ships about 26 m up to Gatun Lake and back down on the other side.
At the spring and fall equinoxes, shadows on the main Maya pyramid look like a serpent crawling down the steps.
Rio was Brazil's capital until 1960. The Christ the Redeemer statue has looked over the city since 1931.

q: Where does the Amazon River flow into the Atlantic Ocean?
fact: The Amazon pours about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.
Shared by Peru and Bolivia, it lies at about 3,810 m. The Uros people live on floating islands made of reeds.

q: Where is the Salar de Uyuni?
fact: The largest salt flat on Earth covers about 10,000 square km. After rain it turns into a giant mirror of the sky.
Its people carved nearly 1,000 giant stone statues called moai. The island belongs to Chile, 3,500 km away.
Ecuador's islands, about 900 km offshore, are home to giant tortoises. Charles Darwin visited them in 1835.
The world's highest waterfall drops 979 m in all from a flat-topped mountain, with a single plunge of 807 m. Its local name is Kerepakupai Meru.
Before the Panama Canal, sailing ships rounded this stormy cape at the tip of South America to travel between the Atlantic and Pacific.

q: Where is the Perito Moreno Glacier?
fact: Its ice front, about 5 km wide, towers up to some 70 m above Lake Argentino. Huge blocks of ice regularly crash down into the water.
At 6,961 m it is the highest mountain in the Americas, and the highest anywhere outside Asia.
These huge drawings of animals and shapes, scratched into the desert about 2,000 years ago, are best seen from the air.
This great Maya city rises from the rainforest. Its tallest temple is about 70 m high.
The largest city in the United States. The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France, has stood in its harbor since 1886.
This part of Los Angeles is the center of the US film industry. Its famous hillside sign first read 'Hollywoodland'.
Founded in 1872, it was the world's first national park. Its geyser Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes.

q: Where is the Kennedy Space Center?
fact: Apollo 11 left from here in July 1969 and carried the first people to walk on the Moon.

q: Where is New Orleans, the birthplace of jazz?
fact: The city lies near the mouth of the Mississippi River and is famous for its Mardi Gras parades.
Badwater Basin, 86 m below sea level, is the lowest point in North America. The valley also holds the highest air temperature ever officially recorded.

q: Where is the Golden Gate Bridge?
fact: The bridge opened in 1937 at the entrance to San Francisco Bay. Its color is called 'International Orange'.
Vancouver hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics. Canada won 14 gold medals there, a record for a Winter Games at the time.
Only about 82 km of sea separate Russia and Alaska here. Its two Diomede Islands lie 4 km apart, but on different sides of the date line.
This giant sandstone rock rises 348 m above the desert. It is sacred to the Anangu, its Aboriginal owners.

q: Where is the Sydney Opera House?
fact: Danish architect Jorn Utzon designed its shell-shaped roofs. The building opened in 1973.

q: Where is Cairns, gateway to the Great Barrier Reef?
fact: The reef is the largest coral reef system in the world, stretching for more than 2,300 km along Australia's coast.
Melbourne hosts the Australian Open tennis every January. Its cricket ground holds about 100,000 people.
Perth is one of the most isolated big cities on Earth: the nearest city of over a million people, Adelaide, is about 2,100 km away.
These limestone stacks were carved by the Southern Ocean off the Great Ocean Road. Despite the name, there were never twelve.
Tasmania's capital is a base for Antarctic expeditions. Founded in 1804, it is the second-oldest of Australia's state capitals, after Sydney.
Despite its name it is a fjord, carved by glaciers. It is one of the wettest places in New Zealand, so waterfalls are everywhere.
Geysers, bubbling mud pools and hot springs surround this town, which is also a center of Maori culture.
New Zealand's highest mountain, 3,724 m. Edmund Hillary trained here before he climbed Everest.
New Zealand's largest city is not its capital. It is built on a field of about 50 small volcanoes.

q: Where is Waitangi, where New Zealand's founding treaty was signed?
fact: The Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand's founding document, was signed here in 1840. Waitangi Day on February 6 is the national day.

q: Where is Taveuni, the Fijian island where you can stand on the 180th meridian?
fact: You can stand with one foot on each side of the 180th meridian here. The date line bends around Fiji, so the whole country keeps one date.
At about 4,509 m it is the highest mountain in Papua New Guinea. Even higher peaks stand in the Indonesian west of the same island.

q: Where is Point Nemo, the place in the ocean farthest from any land?
fact: The nearest land is about 2,700 km away. Old satellites and space stations are steered to crash into the sea near here.

q: Where do the Equator and the Prime Meridian cross?
fact: The point, 0 degrees latitude and 0 degrees longitude, lies in the Atlantic Ocean in the Gulf of Guinea, about 600 km off the coast of Ghana.

q: Where is the Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the ocean?
fact: Nearly 11,000 m deep in the Mariana Trench. If Mount Everest were dropped in, its peak would still be more than 2 km under water.

q: Where is Tristan da Cunha, the most remote inhabited island group?
fact: Fewer than 300 people live there. The nearest other inhabited island, Saint Helena, is about 2,400 km away.
